overview.text: The Niagara Frontier Transportation Authority proposes a 6.4-mile Light Rail Rapid Transit (LRRT) system along Main Street in Buffalo, running 5.2 miles in subway and 1.2 miles at-grade between SUNY-Buffalo's South Campus and Memorial Auditorium, with 14 stations and an estimated cost of $336,250,000. The corridor passes through Buffalo neighborhoods spanning a wide range of incomes—from low-income, highly transit-dependent areas like Ellicott and Masten to higher-income areas like Elmwood—where corridor residents are much more transit-dependent than the regional average. Alternatives evaluated included an Improved Bus 'No Action' plan, advanced bus systems, a bus subway, commuter railroad, heavy rail transit, and multiple light rail and LRRT configurations, with the Minimum LRRT System ranked first. Long-term beneficial impacts include improved CBD accessibility, regional economic stimulation, energy savings, and reduced auto traffic, while adverse impacts include property takings, construction-related noise, dust, and traffic disruption, and visual intrusion from at-grade stations and overhead catenary lines. Public response has been largely favorable following extensive community participation since 1969, with the 1974 hearing yielding nearly all favorable comment and the August 1976 capital grant hearing also drawing favorable response, though earlier opposition to aerial construction led to its elimination.

project_description.text: The Niagara Frontier Transportation Authority proposes a 6.4-mile Light Rail Rapid Transit (LRRT) system along Main Street in the Buffalo-Amherst Corridor, with 5.2 miles in subway and 1.2 miles at-grade ending at Memorial Auditorium. The system will include 14 stations, electrically-propelled lightweight rail vehicles comparable to the Boeing Vertol U.S. Standard LRV, and a service yard south of the CBD, while Main Street between Tupper and Church Streets will become an auto-free pedestrian mall. Total estimated project cost is $336,250,000, funded 80% Federal/20% Local (NY State).

evidence.quote: The Niagara Frontier Transportation Authority of New York (NFTA) has filed an application with UMTA for Federal capital grant assistance to construct and equip a 6.4-mile Light Rail Rapid Transit (LRRT) System along Main Street in the Buffalo-Amherst Corridor, New York.

The proposed LRRT would run in subway for 5.2 miles between the South Campus of the State University of New York at Buffalo and Tupper Street, and at-grade for 1.2 miles from Tupper Street to Buffalo's Memorial Auditorium.

Fourteen stations will be constructed, eight underground, and six at-grade. Three locations near the southern terminus of the proposed rail line are currently under consideration as service and storage yards
The system will utilize electrically-propelled lightweight rail vehicles comparable to the U.S. Standard Light Rail Vehicle (LRV) as now being manufactured by the Boeing Vertol Company.
In conjunction with this project, Main Street between Tupper and Church Streets will be developed as an auto-free pedestrian mall.
The total project cost is estimated at $336,250,000. The requested Federal grant is $269,000,000.

affected_community.text: Buffalo is the 27th largest SMSA in the U.S., located at the eastern end of Lake Erie, with the city experiencing population decline since 1970 and population shifts to the suburbs. Within the transit corridor study area, blacks accounted for close to half of the total population in 1970, and corridor residents are much more transit-dependent than the SMSA average, with the lowest family incomes concentrated in the Ellicott and Masten sub-areas. The line traverses neighborhoods spanning a wide range of incomes, from low-income Ellicott to higher-income Elmwood (which has a high proportion of elderly), and includes important community facilities such as Buffalo General Hospital and Roswell Park Memorial Institute. Buffalo also records the greatest average annual snowfall of any large U.S. city, making reliable mass transit attractive.

alternatives_overview.text: Alternatives evaluated included an Improved Bus 'No Action' plan, advanced bus-based systems with bus-only lanes, a bus subway, commuter railroad (deemed infeasible), and various rail rapid transit options including a benchmark 11-mile heavy rail transit system, modified HRT systems, and nine LRT and five LRRT systems with various extensions. The Bus Subway was rejected for costing over $180 million more than the benchmark HRT, and major highway expansion was determined no longer viable. A two-stage screening process (economic, then level-of-service/social/environmental) ranked the Minimum LRRT System first, and three sites—South, Ellicott, and Terminal—are under consideration for the service and storage yard.

environmental_impact.text: Long-term beneficial effects include improved CBD accessibility, regional economic stimulation, modest direct energy savings of about 4.7% over the bus alternative, and approximately 2,500 fewer autos driven into the CBD each day in 1995. Adverse impacts include taking of approximately 21 parcels along Main Street with 8 structures razed, additional takings depending on the service yard site (with the South Yard requiring 7.7 acres of private land and 22 structures razed), and visual intrusion from at-grade stations and overhead catenary lines. Air quality effects show modest decreases in carbon monoxide, hydrocarbons, and particulates accompanied by a modest increase in nitrogen oxide emissions. Construction will cause temporary traffic congestion, fugitive dust, exhaust odors, and noise, while operational noise and vibration will be mitigated through continuous welded rail, resilient fasteners, and floating slab trackbeds.

public_response.text: The proposed project has been the subject of extensive discussion and review with public and local officials since 1969, with public hearings held in April 1972 and July 1974, the latter yielding nearly all favorable comment. Earlier community opposition to portions of the original alignment and significant lengths of aerial structure necessitated a project re-evaluation, and citizen rejection eliminated the concept of aerial construction along Main Street. Citizen committees including the Joint Executive Committee for Rapid Transit and the Committee for Federal Action were formed to support the project, and the August 1976 hearing on the capital grant application drew favorable response. The Buffalo Landmark and Preservation Board found no problems with the project, and UMTA planned an additional public hearing for July 14, 1977.
